extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, practicing journalists, and general readers interested in how national news is selected and presented
extracted.subtask_description: Qualitative and limited quantitative content-analysis framework for studying what national television evening news and newsmagazines select as 'news' (actors and activities) and how they structure it. Focuses on selection patterns, actor/activity categories, and methodological choices for coding and sampling.

rubrics_metrics.name: News program structure and time constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Half-hour television evening news programs actually contain 22-23 minutes of news, combine filmed (often taped) stories with 'tell stories' presented by anchorpersons, and are divided into four or five sections interrupted by commercials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically: five or six filmed 'hard' news stories (1–2 minutes each), one or two longer 'features', and about 6 minutes of tell stories (15–30 seconds each) that introduce, update, and provide headline summaries. When major events occur, the normal daily format may be set aside and 8–10 minutes or more can be given to one story.

rubrics_metrics.name: News structured like a newspaper (lead and order)
rubrics_metrics.description: The news program is structured like a newspaper: the day's most important story is the lead and the first two sections are generally devoted to the other important hard news of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features often occupy remaining sections and programs often end with an amusing human-interest anecdote. Normal format can be altered for world-shaking events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell stories function
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tell stories’ are short anchor-presented segments that introduce and end film stories, update them, and provide headline service for items not suitable for filming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They take up about 6 minutes of each program and run 15–30 seconds each; help summarize foreign or domestic stories that do not lend themselves to filming or are not deemed sufficiently important for film.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsmagazine structure and section importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsmagazines run ~50 pages weekly, combine dramatic narrative and pictures (pictures often take at least a third of the newshole), and classify news into regularly appearing titled sections: 'front of the book' (national/international/business) and multiple 'back-of-the-book' sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most important section to editors is the weekly cover story (announced on the cover); cover stories may appear anywhere but front and back sections are usually divided by a gossip/people section; back sections appear less frequently and may include reviews and specialty beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition effects on content
rubrics_metrics.description: By and large the three newscasts and the two newsmagazines report roughly the same stories, though competition causes differences and innovations (e.g., CBS commentaries, NBC 'Segment 3', ABC interviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competition influences format and emphases (e.g., more investigative segments, de-emphasizing anchors, featuring major reporters, running book excerpts) and may shift the concept of newsweeklies away from a traditional 'magazine of record.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for individuals over groups or processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists often say news ought to be about individuals rather than groups or social processes; most news is indeed about individuals, even when those individuals are in conflict with groups or impersonal forces like 'inflation' or 'communism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This selection tendency shapes what becomes news and implies many social processes are underrepresented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowns vs Unknowns (actor-type distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors who appear in the news are classified as 'Knowns' (well-known people or those occupying well-known positions) or 'Unknowns' (ordinary people prototypical of groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the author's samples Knowns occupied 70–85% of domestic news while Unknowns about a fifth; remainder were animals, objects, abstractions. Known/Unknown classification affects who is reported and how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Knowns — Incumbent presidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Incumbent presidents are the single individual appearing most often in the news; he normally appears in every issue of the newsmagazine and on virtually all television news programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike others, his routine activities are deemed routinely newsworthy; in sample years he occupied a large percent of magazine space and television news time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Knowns — Presidential candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidential candidates (affiliated with one of the two major parties) enter the news once they act like candidates and remain newsworthy while they appear to have a chance at the nomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During election years, candidates can obtain more space/time than incumbents; magazines may start coverage well before television does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Knowns — Leading federal officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Leading federal officials (leaders of House and Senate, major committee heads, selected cabinet members) appear frequently; certain cabinet posts (secretary of state, treasury) get more coverage depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: White House staff surfaced more after Watergate; the Supreme Court usually appears as a group unless individual justices are appointed/retire; agency heads enter news when announcing new policy or in conflict with the president.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Knowns — State and local officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonfederal officials in the news are mostly governors and mayors of large states/cities, appearing when their offices become relevant to national concerns (e.g., unrest, fiscal crises, school bussing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Election of black mayors or actions with national resonance can make local officials national news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Knowns — Alleged and actual violators (Known violators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-known people who get into legal or moral trouble (or ordinary people who commit dramatic crimes) become Knowns because of their offenses; Knowns dominate coverage of violators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage often focuses on trials and investigations; in some years (e.g., Watergate) Knowns accounted for a very large share of violator coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Unknowns — Protesters, 'rioters', and strikers
rubrics_metrics.description: Unknowns most often appear when they act in opposition to government policies (protests, disturbances, strikes); in certain years a large fraction of ordinary people in the news were protesters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition changes over time (e.g., 1960s: black participants in ghetto disturbances; 1970s: protests over school/residential integration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Unknowns — Victims
rubrics_metrics.description: Unknowns appear as victims of natural or social disorders (crime, disasters) and as victims of bureaucracy or economic dislocation (unemployment), and are regularly covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television emphasizes victims of disasters; magazine coverage previously emphasized victims of ghetto disturbances and later victims of unemployment or bureaucracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Unknowns — Alleged and actual violators (Unknown violators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unknowns who get in trouble (kidnappers, mass murderers, grisly individual killers) are reported, usually focusing on actions more than trials; their victims are often Unknowns as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unknown violators tend to be accused of different crimes than Knowns; nonviolent unknown offenders rarely make national news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Unknowns — Participants in unusual activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Unknowns gain newsworthiness by engaging in bizarre fads, exotic cults, unusual hobbies, or departing from expected roles (e.g., elderly acting youthful), producing 'man-bites-dog' human-interest stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features like Charles Kuralt's 'On the Road' often highlight such Unknowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Unknowns — Voters, poll respondents, and aggregates
rubrics_metrics.description: Unknowns also enter the news as statistical or aggregate categories (voters, poll respondents, unemployed, consumers) rather than as named individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of poll data and aggregates has increased; nonstatistical aggregates (e.g., nonprotesting parents) also appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activities-in-news taxonomy (major activities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis categorizes news by the activities reported rather than topics: government conflicts and disagreements; government decisions/proposals/ceremonies; government personnel changes (including campaigning); protests (violent and nonviolent); crimes/scandals/investigations; disasters (actual and averted); innovation and tradition; rites of passage (births, weddings, deaths); biographies (magazines); unusual activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eight are identified as most frequent/important; combining protest with intragovernment conflict yields political conflict as the single most frequent activity; relative percentages vary by year and medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government conflicts and disagreements as a newscategory
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately 15% of domestic news is disagreements and conflicts within and between parts of government and public officials, often featuring the president's disputes with Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific conflict topics vary over time (e.g., economic policy since 1970s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Government decisions, proposals, and ceremonies as a newscategory
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that report government decisions, proposals, and ceremonies (announcements of new policies, congressional approval, Supreme Court decisions) form a distinct activity class; some journalists call these 'input' stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Output stories—actual implementation—appear much more rarely in the news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government personnel changes and campaigning as a newscategory
rubrics_metrics.description: Personnel-change stories (appointments, resignations, dismissals, campaign activities of presidential hopefuls) are numerically frequent in newsmagazines and form a specific category of government news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television may underemphasize pre-election campaigning outside election years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crimes, scandals, and investigations as a newscategory
rubrics_metrics.description: Crimes, scandals, and related investigations make up a large portion (around a fifth in some samples) of domestic activities covered; in certain years (e.g., Watergate/CIA) they can be the most newsworthy topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical stories often concern financial misbehavior of government officials and associated trials/investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-analysis methodology — unit of analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The unit of analysis was the individual story (for both television and magazine), classified by the actor and activity that dominated it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two or more actors/activities dominated, the story was split over the relevant categories by the amount of time or space given to each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-analysis methodology — sampling choices and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The qualitative analysis was based on over ten years of observation supplemented by quantitative data from a six-month sample of stories appearing in alternate months during 1967, 1971, and 1975 (with some 1969 data); the quantitative analysis omitted the Vietnam War and domestic news directly connected with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Years chosen to avoid presidential election years; television scripts sampled from CBS (complete scripts available); magazine chosen by coin flip (Newsweek). Omission of war-related news affects findings and is noted throughout the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-analysis methodology — coding and category construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories were deliberately general to abstract specific stories from contexts (e.g., all protests grouped together), calling attention to similarities between electronic and print media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalization means the resulting picture is not the only one possible; concepts and categories contain values and value implications; findings are thus analytic rather than purely critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement note — stories count vs minutes/columns
rubrics_metrics.description: For the broad categories used, counting number of stories produced percentages almost identical to analyses by minutes (television) or columns (magazines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author limited analysis to story counts because more granular measures were unnecessary given category breadth; analyzing TV scripts was time-consuming so only one year was done for TV minutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection bias implication — what is left out
rubrics_metrics.description: Because journalists must select from innumerable events, recurring patterns emerge and many routines of ordinary people (family life, work outside newsworthy events) rarely appear; omissions are part of the analytic critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analyst also examined what is left out of the news; audience interpretation may differ from the picture the analyst sketches.
